series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.1 · October 2026
title: Price Production and Consumption Separately

slides.title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
slides.subtitle: A two-track architecture for carbon pricing in open economies
slides.message: One carbon price does two jobs, and in an open economy the second undermines the first. Price production with a revenue-neutral feebate and consumption at the destination: the full carbon price signal, without leakage and at no cost to the treasury.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: In an open economy, one price does two jobs and the second undermines the first

points.lead: Job 1: cut emissions per tonne of output.
points.text: A carbon tax on producers does this well.

points.lead: Job 2: make buyers pay for carbon.
points.text: The tax raises the price of everything the country makes, so buyers use less.
Part of the fall in home output is replaced by foreign supply: leakage, 5–25% of the emission cut in model studies, concentrated in steel, cement and other trade-exposed industries.

points.lead: So governments exempt industry or keep the rate low.
points.text: A border charge on imports (the EU's CBAM) protects the home market but leaves exports carrying the bill.

slides.source: Branger and Quirion (2014); Keen, Parry and Roaf (2022).

slides.title: Two tracks: price production by intensity, consumption at the destination
slides.caption: Carbon-related cost per tonne of steel at $80/tCO₂ (stylized: home mill at Türkiye's default intensity, foreign at China's).

points.text: a feebate. Pay on emissions per tonne above the sector average, rebate below. Payments cancel; the full marginal incentive stays.
a carbon component of VAT, imports charged, exports exempt; plus a forward obligation on fuel suppliers.
the cost of the abatement itself.

slides.title: A feebate raises exporters' costs about a third as much as a tax at the same rate
slides.note: A tax charges for every tonne still emitted; a feebate only for the cost of cutting. The most carbon-intensive exporters gain most from choosing a feebate.
slides.source: EU default values (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621); base price $600/t and abatement costs stylized. Working paper 1.1, Table 1.

slides.title: The feebate gives no reason to consume less; the consumption track supplies it, without leakage

points.text: Alone, a feebate needs a higher rate than a tax to cut the same tonnes, because it barely raises the average price.
charges home-made and imported goods alike, so buying abroad gains nothing. The value part of VAT can fall as the carbon part rises.
is covered by a legal obligation on the few large suppliers, announced years ahead so investors know the price.
The production rate can be high because it barely raises costs; the consumption rate is set by what households accept.

slides.title: Climate finance above half the feebate rate makes adoption a gain for the country

points.lead: Average cost is half the marginal cost:
points.text: the cheapest cuts come first.

points.lead: So a payment above half the rate pays,
points.text: and the country's best feebate rate equals the payment.
a whole sector's measured intensity, not contested single installations. Under an Article 6 transfer the threshold rises to about 1.5 times the rate.

slides.source: Author's calculation, steel at Türkiye's default intensity, payment $50/tCO₂; Strand (2020).

slides.title: Border charges set by country and sector turn leakage into a race to the top
slides.caption: Simulated steel import market, eight exporters at EU default intensities (prices and costs stylized).

points.lead: No mill can move its country's charge;
points.text: a national feebate can. The best feebate rate equals the charge.
import carbon falls 28% through supplier mix alone, 70% when exporters respond.

points.lead: Today's CBAM credits only a price paid,
points.text: so a feebate earns nothing. Credit carbon-price equivalents.

slides.title: The design rides on systems that already exist

points.text: the feebate needs sector output, plant emissions and a benchmark rule. The CBAM already defines plant measurement in six sectors.
the consumption charge needs a working VAT. Countries without one can run the feebate first, where most of their emissions are.
a charge levied alike on imports and home goods, exports exempt, follows border adjustment of internal taxes; the feebate's rebate leg needs careful drafting.
measure the net effect of the VAT shift on poorer households before setting the rate.

slides.source: Working paper 1.1, Sections 8–9; Mehling et al. (2019).
